cues.text: On January 29, 1568, a cloth shearer named Joan Prats, struggling with poverty, broke into his own parish church in Alcoy, Spain.
He stole a silver ciborium holding forty consecrated Hosts, along with a pyx and a reliquary—sacred vessels worth considerably more than the man's ordinary means.
A Statue That Pointed the Way
The theft was discovered quickly, and the town's search for the stolen vessels turned on an unexpected sign, according to Alcoy's tradition.
A statue of the Child Jesus was reported to point toward the location where Prats had concealed his stolen goods, leading searchers directly to the hiding place.
The consecrated Hosts were recovered from where Prats had hidden them.
The theft was resolved with unusual speed for an era when such crimes often went unsolved for months or longer.
In local memory, it became less a story of the crime itself than of the swiftness and strangeness of its resolution.
The house where Prats had committed the theft was later converted into an oratory.
It remains open to visitors in Alcoy today, physically tying the town’s devotion to the building where the sacrilege occurred, rather than only to the church it was taken from.
Every year on January 31, the people of Alcoy hold a solemn procession: the Procession of the Miraculous Baby Jesus, or Jesuset del Miracle in the local Valencian tongue.
It commemorates the 1568 theft and its resolution, a devotion now more than four and a half centuries old.

The Alcoy tradition, like several other Spanish accounts from this same turbulent century, frames its central image not as punishment for the thief but as a statue's silent, specific guidance toward setting the theft right.
